title: Clustered vs. Non-Clustered Indexes and Heap Tables
description: Clustered vs. Non-Clustered Indexes and Heap Tables. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Explain logical index order versus physical row order.
Describe PostgreSQL heap tuples and TIDs.
Compare clustered-index engines with PostgreSQL CLUSTER.

mentalModel.text: An index's logical order does not automatically determine table-row storage order. PostgreSQL normally stores tuples in a heap and index entries point to tuple locations. CLUSTER rewrites a table in index order once, but later writes can erode that order.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL stores ordinary rows in heap pages. An index entry normally points to a heap tuple through a TID identifying its page and slot. The heap is not automatically sorted by every index.

blocks.title: Key distinctions
rows: Structure used to locate candidate rows

blocks.text: In a clustered-index engine, table data is organized at the clustered key's leaf level. PostgreSQL normally uses a heap plus indexes pointing to TIDs. Terminology is database-specific.

steps.title: Identify query shape
steps.description: Write down predicates, joins, ordering, limit, and selected columns.

steps.title: Predict the mechanism
steps.description: Explain which pages, entries, or operators the database is likely to visit.

steps.title: Validate the plan
steps.description: Use actual rows and buffers to compare prediction with observed work.

blocks.text: Nearby index keys stored in nearby heap pages can reduce pages visited. Scattered matching rows can make an index scan trigger many random heap fetches.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CLUSTER orders USING orders_created_at_idx; ANALYZE orders;

blocks.problem: A query is slower than expected even though an index exists.
reasoning: Check whether index keys and predicates align.
Compare estimated and actual row counts and inspect buffers.
Account for result size, heap access, and write/storage trade-offs.
blocks.outcome: Make a targeted change only after plan evidence supports the hypothesis.

blocks.text: An index-only scan can return stored values from the index, but PostgreSQL must still establish tuple visibility. The visibility map lets it skip heap visits for all-visible pages; otherwise heap fetches can remain.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_cover_idx ON orders (customer_id,created_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_amount);

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.text: Physical clustering can help locality-sensitive range reads, but requires a rewrite and its benefit decays. A covering index can reduce some heap access if output and visibility-map conditions permit.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT created_at,total_amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 1
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Physical order is not logical index order: a PostgreSQL heap is not automatically sorted by each B-tree.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 2
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: INCLUDE can help index-only retrieval but adds storage and write costs.

revisionSheet.text: PostgreSQL ordinary indexes reference heap tuple locations.
CLUSTER rewrites a PostgreSQL table once.
INCLUDE can help index-only retrieval but adds storage and write costs.
Visibility-map state and heap locality affect actual performance.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, an ordinary B-tree index entry generally points to what?

options.text: A heap tuple location (TID)
A permanent row position that never changes
A table page sorted by that index
The entire row stored in every index

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL heap tuples are addressed by TIDs; locations can change after updates or rewrites.

questions.prompt: What is a clustered index in a clustered-index engine?

options.text: The table data is organized at the leaf level by the clustered key
A separate copy unrelated to row storage
An index that never affects secondary-index size
Identical to PostgreSQL's default heap arrangement

questions.explanation: Clustered-index terminology refers to the data organization in engines such as SQL Server.

options.text: Rewrites a table in the order of a chosen index at that time
Maintains sorted order after every future insert
Creates an index without touching table rows
Makes the heap immutable

questions.explanation: CLUSTER is a one-time physical reorganization.

questions.prompt: Why can locality help a range query?

options.text: Nearby keys may require fewer distinct heap pages
It guarantees all results are cached
It removes MVCC checks forever
It removes query planning

questions.explanation: Locality can reduce page reads but does not eliminate other work.

questions.prompt: What does INCLUDE do in PostgreSQL B-tree?

options.text: Stores non-key payload that may cover output columns
Makes payload columns first in search order
Guarantees no heap fetches in every case
Adds uniqueness to included values

questions.explanation: INCLUDE can support index-only scans but enlarges the index.

questions.prompt: An index finds 500 rows scattered across 400 heap pages. What is the concern?

options.text: Heap I/O may dominate despite efficient index navigation
The B-tree must be rebuilt because 500 is not logarithmic
The query cannot return more than one row
PostgreSQL sorts the heap after every SELECT

questions.explanation: Scattered heap fetches can dominate latency.

questions.prompt: Why not use a TID as a durable business identifier?

options.text: It is a physical tuple location and can change
It is always the primary key
It is globally stable forever
PostgreSQL indexes do not use TIDs

questions.explanation: TIDs are physical locations, not stable application identity.

questions.prompt: When might CLUSTER be worth considering?

options.text: Measured range-read locality is a bottleneck and rewrite/locking costs are acceptable
For every table because all queries speed up
Only when no indexes exist
To enforce uniqueness

questions.explanation: Clustering can improve locality for some workloads but has operational costs.

questions.prompt: Which statements about PostgreSQL heap/index behavior are correct?

options.text: Ordinary index entries generally point to heap tuple locations.
Heap rows are automatically sorted by every B-tree.
Index-only scans may still fetch heap tuples.
CLUSTER continuously preserves order after future writes.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL uses heap storage; index-only scans depend on visibility, and CLUSTER is not continuous.

questions.prompt: Which are costs or limits of INCLUDE columns?

options.text: Larger index footprint
More write maintenance
They change key ordering
Visibility-map state may still require heap fetches

questions.explanation: Included payload increases size and maintenance and may help index-only scans, but is not key ordering.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL heap rows are automatically kept in the order of every B-tree index.
questions.explanation: Heap storage is independent of each index's logical order.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL CLUSTER guarantees future inserts stay in the chosen index order.
questions.explanation: It rewrites the table once; future writes can erode order.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A range report has many heap buffers despite using an index. How reason about clustering or covering?
strongAnswerPoints: Inspect actual rows, buffers, correlation, and visibility-map behavior.
Check whether a covering index can contain required output.
Explain rewrite locking and that CLUSTER does not preserve order continuously.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Verify the plan first. Scattered heap access may dominate. A covering index can help when visibility conditions permit; CLUSTER can improve locality but rewrites and locks the table and its benefit decays as rows change.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Explain clustered versus non-clustered indexes to a team using PostgreSQL and SQL Server.
strongAnswerPoints: Separate logical index order from physical table storage.
Describe SQL Server clustered data organization versus PostgreSQL heap plus TID references.
Mention CLUSTER as a one-time rewrite.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: In SQL Server a clustered index organizes table data at the clustered key's leaf level; nonclustered indexes use a clustered key or RID as locator. PostgreSQL normally uses a heap and B-tree entries pointing to TIDs. CLUSTER rewrites the heap once, not continuously.
